speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: asked the Minister for Education what is the Ministry's current position on optimal class sizes given recent findings that teachers face increasing complexity in their roles, including supporting students with diverse learning needs, mental health challenges and special educational needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Primary 1 and 2 students learn in class sizes of around 30.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because they have just started their educational journey and we want to be able to better support in that transition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: TRANsition Support for InTegration (TRANSIT) classes, conducted in even smaller class sizes of up to 10.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because TRANSIT classes help our Primary 1 students who are identified with social and behavioural needs to develop foundational self-management skills when they start schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, recently, I sat in one of these TRANSIT classes to see how they carry out the approach, pedagogical as well as socio-emotional learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Another example is the Learning Support Programme, conducted in pull-out classes of around eight to 10.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because this is a specialised early intervention programme in our schools for lower primary students who need additional help with the English language.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: School-based Dyslexia Remediation Programme, conducted in classes of four to six students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because with these special education needs, we want to better support them, because overcoming some of these challenges or managing these challenges, like dyslexia, allows them to access support for many other subjects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: With Full Subject-Based Banding, our secondary school students attend different subject classes of between 20 and 40 students, depending on their learning needs and the nature of the subject.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Additionally, schools may deploy two form teachers for classes on a needs basis where school resourcing allows.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will continue to study the effectiveness of our approach, including on class sizes and are prepared to adjust our strategies where necessary to create conducive learning environments for our students.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is heartening to know that MOE is already taking good steps in this direction.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wanted to ask the Minister, does the Minister agree that in a world with artificial intelligence (AI) disrupting the learning of content in a nation of smaller family sizes, it is even more important that children learn the soft skills which no machine can teach, and develop emotional and psychological strengths which only humans can nurture?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And given that human mentoring and the learning of soft skills cannot scale so easily with technology, will MOE relook class sizes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, in our AI in education framework, we want to teach our children what is AI, how to use AI, how to learn with AI and most importantly, how to learn beyond AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, through the 21st Century Competencies Framework, which was recently enhanced, we seek to provide support and strengthen our children's learning of these important values and skills through a combination of weaving through academic subjects through co-curricular activities (CCA), Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) and other forms of support in school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this means that teaching is not just academic teaching of subjects, but also more holistic teaching of a child and empowering them with 21st century competencies and social-emotional learning through activities like CCA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, with this in mind, we continue to see how best to support our children, and by putting more resources for students with greater needs, we ensure that they get more holistic support – not just through teaching support, but also support of Special Educational Needs Officers and counselling support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand, as the Minister has shared, that advances in learning technology, especially AI, now afford customised education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But based on this research, it seems like such customised education is not a justifiable substitute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I wonder if the Ministry will therefore look at alternatives other than purely reducing class sizes, such as the possibility of increasing allied teachers or teaching assistants within the classroom?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if so, what the Minister has to share with regard to the decision by the Ministry to scale back on allied educators when it comes to teaching and learning?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member makes a very good observation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member is also absolutely right that edtech is important.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In that regard, edtech is never a substitute for the human touch, and I would like to thank the Member for being so supportive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And I thank the Minister for his responses to the questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And my question is, is there some sort of a threshold or target that helps school leaders or MOE determine when there is enough resources to support their students in this regard?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, this is a continuous conversation between our school leaders, who are in touch with the ground, in close contact with their teachers in the classroom, as well as their MOE headquarters (HQ) leadership – our superintendent, zonal directors, director of schools and the HQ in general – to better understand the specific needs of different schools and to be able to allocate resources accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, there is baseline support in terms of teaching, allied resources and admin staff for each school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But there may be needs in particular schools that require us to deploy, say, more counsellors or more student welfare officers or more special educational needs officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And some of these resources are not just school-based, but also cluster-based, giving flexibility to school leaders to be able to ask and get more resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But ultimately, whether it is class sizes or other forms of resources, basically, our mission in MOE is this: we have our resources; we also have to operate within constraints, because MOE does not operate our budget independently of other Ministries' needs and Singapore's needs, as well as the opportunities that are presented to us, such as new studies, new pedagogical methods, new methods to impart social-emotional learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How do we optimise between our resources, operate within constraints and the opportunities we seize?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And to talk about class sizes, if we were to increase the number of teachers, then we need to operate within the constraint of the impact on other important sectors that serve society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also need to make sure that in hiring many more teachers, our profession reminds us that we must uphold standards and quality of the whole profession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if we were to increase the number of classes that teachers teach, then, in managing overall workload and impact, we will then have to recalibrate and reimagine what teachers do on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In some countries teachers teach many more classes, partially because of workload and resourcing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But if in Singapore, if we were to do that, it would probably have to be a combination of three things: one, increasing recruitment; two, increasing the number of classes that teachers teach; and then, recalibrating the other things that teachers do – CCA, CCE, admin, class preparation, marking and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And lastly, of course, harnessing technology tools, including AI, to empower teacher to do so much more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The classroom of today is very different from the classroom of our time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can continue to see progress and changes; and I would say three things are on the horizon that will allow us to try to transform education to make Singapore ready for a very uncertain future, one that is still full of opportunity and hope.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One, would be the review that we announced recently, the education conversations that we hold across Singapore to allow us to relook at the academic race, the "arms race", so that we focus on deep learning and not academic pursuits through high stakes exams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in the same vein, we look at holistic education through a review of CCE and CCA, so we see it in totality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The other, of course, is the AI in education framework that I mentioned.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it is not just about edtech and tools, but how do we reimagine teaching in an era where AI can do certain things, do more things and how can people remain on top as masters of technology?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, these are the areas that we are looking at.
